In [[probability theory]], [[statistics]], and [[machine learning]], the '''continuous Bernoulli distribution'''<ref>Loaiza-Ganem, G., & Cunningham, J. P. (2019). The continuous Bernoulli: fixing a pervasive error in variational autoencoders. In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (pp. 13266-13276).</ref><ref>PyTorch Distributions. https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributions.html#continuousbernoulli</ref><ref>Tensorflow Probability. https://www.tensorflow.org/probability/api_docs/python/tfp/edward2/ContinuousBernoulli {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201125001136/https://www.tensorflow.org/probability/api_docs/python/tfp/edward2/ContinuousBernoulli |date=2020-11-25 }}</ref> is a family of continuous [[probability distribution]]s  parameterized by a single [[shape parameter]] <math>\lambda \in (0, 1)</math>, defined on the unit interval <math>x \in [0, 1]</math>, by:
:<math> p(x | \lambda) \propto \lambda^x (1-\lambda)^{1-x}. </math>

The continuous Bernoulli distribution arises in [[deep learning]] and [[computer vision]], specifically in the context of [[variational autoencoder]]s,<ref>Kingma, D. P., & Welling, M. (2013). Auto-encoding variational bayes. arXiv preprint arXiv:1312.6114.</ref><ref>Kingma, D. P., & Welling, M. (2014, April). Stochastic gradient VB and the variational auto-encoder. In Second International Conference on Learning Representations, ICLR (Vol. 19).</ref> for modeling the pixel intensities of natural images. As such, it defines a proper probabilistic counterpart for the commonly used binary [[cross entropy]] loss, which is often applied to continuous, <math>[0,1]</math>-valued data.<ref>Larsen, A. B. L., Sønderby, S. K., Larochelle, H., & Winther, O. (2016, June). Autoencoding beyond pixels using a learned similarity metric. In International conference on machine learning (pp. 1558-1566).</ref><ref>Jiang, Z., Zheng, Y., Tan, H., Tang, B., & Zhou, H. (2017, August). Variational deep embedding: an unsupervised and generative approach to clustering. In Proceedings of the 26th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (pp. 1965-1972).</ref><ref>PyTorch VAE tutorial: https://github.com/pytorch/examples/tree/master/vae.</ref><ref>Keras VAE tutorial: https://blog.keras.io/building-autoencoders-in-keras.html.</ref> This practice amounts to ignoring the normalizing constant of the continuous Bernoulli distribution, since the binary cross entropy loss only defines a true log-likelihood for discrete, <math>\{0,1\}</math>-valued data.

The continuous Bernoulli also defines an [[exponential family]] of distributions. Writing <math>\theta = \log\left(\lambda/(1-\lambda)\right)</math> for the [[natural parameter]], the density can be rewritten in canonical form:
<math> p(x | \theta) \propto \exp (\theta x) </math>. <ref name="Lee2025">Lee, C. J.; Dahl, B. K.; Ovaskainen, O.; Dunson, D. B. (2026). ''Scalable and robust regression models for continuous proportional data''. Journal of the American Statistical Association. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.2026.2626081</ref>

== Statistical inference ==

Given an independent sample of <math>n</math> points <math>x_1,\dots,x_n</math> with <math>x_i\in[0,1]\,\forall i</math> from continuous Bernoulli, the log-likelihood of the natural parameter <math>\theta</math> is
:<math>\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \theta \sum_{i=1}^n x_i - n \log \{(e^\theta - 1)/\theta\}</math>
and the [[maximum likelihood estimator]] of the natural parameter <math>\theta</math> is the solution of <math> \mathcal{L}'(\theta) =0 </math>, that is, <math> \hat{\theta} </math> satisfies
:<math> \frac{e^{\hat{\theta}}}{e^{\hat{\theta}} - 1} - \frac{1}{\hat{\theta}}= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i</math>
where the left hand side <math>e^{\hat{\theta}}/(e^{\hat{\theta}} - 1) - \hat{\theta}^{-1}</math> is the expected value of continuous Bernoulli with parameter <math> \hat\theta </math>. Although <math> \hat{\theta} </math> does not admit a closed-form expression, it can be easily calculated with numerical inversion.


== Further properties == 



The entropy of a continuous Bernoulli distribution is
:<math>\operatorname{H}[X] = \begin{cases} 0 &\text{ if } \lambda = \frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{\lambda\log\left(\lambda\right) - \left(1 - \lambda\right)\log\left(1 - \lambda\right)}{1 - 2\lambda} - \log\left(\frac{2 \tanh^{-1}\left(1 - 2\lambda\right)}{e\left(1 - 2\lambda\right)}\right)  &\text{ otherwise} \end{cases}\!</math>

== Related distributions ==

=== Bernoulli distribution ===
The continuous Bernoulli can be thought of as a continuous relaxation of the [[Bernoulli distribution]], which is defined on the discrete set <math> \{0,1\} </math> by the [[probability mass function]]:
:<math> p(x) = p^x (1-p)^{1-x}, </math>
where <math> p </math> is a scalar parameter between 0 and 1. Applying this same functional form on the continuous interval <math> [0,1] </math> results in the continuous Bernoulli [[probability density function]], up to a normalizing constant.

=== Uniform distribution ===
The [[Continuous_uniform_distribution|Uniform distribution]] between the unit interval [0,1] is a special case of continuous Bernoulli when <math>\lambda = 1/2</math> or <math>\theta = 0</math>.

=== Exponential distribution ===
An [[exponential distribution]] with rate <math> \Lambda </math> restricted to the unit interval [0,1] corresponds to a continuous Bernoulli distribution with natural parameter <math>\theta = -\Lambda < 0 </math>.

=== Continuous categorical distribution ===
The multivariate generalization of the continuous Bernoulli is called the [[continuous-categorical]].<ref>Gordon-Rodriguez, E., Loaiza-Ganem, G., & Cunningham, J. P. (2020). The continuous categorical: a novel simplex-valued exponential family. In 36th International Conference on Machine Learning, ICML 2020. International Machine Learning Society (IMLS).</ref>
